opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think GDPval matters because a lot of the benchmarks we've relied on have started to saturate, and many of them were never designed to tell us what we actually care about, which is how useful these models are for the work people do every day.

Traditional evals tend to look like exams: multiple-choice questions, competition math, short coding puzzles. Those were great signals for a while, but they're a bit academic. Doing well on a hard test isn't the same as being able to write a legal brief, put together a financial model, or draft a nursing care plan that a real professional would sign off on.

With GDPval we tried to measure that more directly. We looked at the sectors that contribute most to the economy and the occupations within them, then worked with experienced professionals, people with many years in their fields, to create tasks based on their actual work. These aren't toy prompts. They often include reference files, require producing real deliverables like documents, spreadsheets, or slide decks, and can take a human expert hours to complete.

Grading is also done by experts. Professionals in the same occupation compare the model's output against a human expert's output, without knowing which is which, and judge which one they'd prefer. That gives us a much more grounded sense of where models are competitive with professionals and where they still fall short.

So the reason I see it as an important step is that it moves the conversation from "how smart is the model on a test" toward "how much real-world value can it provide." That's useful for us in tracking progress, and it's useful for the public, policymakers, and businesses trying to understand what's coming. It's still a first version. Right now the tasks are one-shot, and real jobs involve iteration, context, and collaboration. But I think it points in the right direction for how we should be evaluating these systems.

r001.rationale: The response says many benchmarks have started to saturate, but does not identify SWE-bench or say saturation obscured improvements between successive models.

r002.rationale: It describes choosing sectors and occupations, but does not mention Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational task listings.

r003.rationale: It says tasks are based on professionals’ actual work and may include reference files, but does not clearly state that models receive the context a worker would have when doing those tasks.

r004.rationale: It says GDPval shifts discussion toward real-world value, but does not credit it with catalyzing greater organizational attention to making models useful for real-world work.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The way I think about it is that for a long time, the benchmarks we used to measure progress were basically academic exams. Things like competition math, coding puzzles, multiple-choice science questions. And those were really useful early on, because they gave us clean, gradable signals. But the models have gotten so good at them that a lot of those evals are saturating, and more importantly, they were never really measuring the thing most people actually care about, which is: can this model do real work? Can it do the kind of task that someone gets paid to do on a Tuesday afternoon?

That's the gap GDPval is trying to close. Instead of asking the model a textbook question, we went out and collected tasks from experienced professionals across a wide range of occupations, chosen based on the sectors that contribute most to GDP. So you have lawyers, nurses, financial analysts, software engineers, manufacturing engineers, salespeople, and so on. And the tasks aren't abstractions. They're things like "draft this legal brief," "build this financial model in a spreadsheet," "produce this engineering diagram," "write up this nursing care plan," with the real reference files and context you'd get on the job. The people who wrote them have, on average, well over a decade of experience, and in many cases it's work they've actually done.

The second piece that I think matters a lot is how we grade it. A lot of these outputs don't have a single right answer. There's no answer key for a good marketing deck. So rather than pretending there is one, we have experts in that same occupation do blind comparisons: here are two deliverables, one from a human professional, one from a model, which one would you rather receive and why? That gives you a measure that's much closer to how the world actually judges work, which is by whether another expert thinks it's good.

And the reason I find that exciting is that it changes the conversation. When a model scores a few points higher on a math benchmark, it's hard for anyone outside the field to know what that means. But when you can say, on these kinds of professional tasks, experts preferred the model's output a certain fraction of the time, and here's where it falls short, that's legible. It's legible to policymakers who want to understand economic impact, it's legible to companies deciding where to deploy these systems, and honestly it's legible to us as researchers, because it tells us where the models are still failing in ways that matter. We saw a lot of failures that weren't about raw intelligence at all. They were about not following instructions precisely, producing something with formatting problems, or being too confident about something that was wrong. Those are exactly the things you'd never catch on a multiple-choice test.

I'd also say we're very upfront that this is a first step, not the finish line. The tasks are still mostly one-shot. You get a prompt and context, you produce a deliverable. Real jobs are much more interactive and much more ambiguous than that, and the hard part of a lot of work is figuring out what to do rather than doing it. So I think of GDPval as moving the goalposts in the right direction: toward evaluations grounded in real economic activity, graded by real experts, that track whether these systems are becoming genuinely useful rather than just impressive. And if we can keep iterating on that, I think we'll have a much more honest picture of where AI actually stands.

r002.rationale: It says tasks were selected based on sectors’ contributions to GDP, but does not identify Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational task listings.

r003.rationale: It describes professional workplace tasks supplied with real reference files and context a worker would have on the job.

r004.rationale: It says GDPval changes the conversation and is legible to companies, but does not clearly credit it with catalyzing greater organizational attention to making models useful for real-world work.

astra-6.text:
I think GDPval is an important step because it brings evaluation closer to what people actually want to use AI for: doing useful work. A model can perform really well on an academic benchmark, but that doesn’t necessarily tell you whether it can produce a useful analysis, put together a presentation, or handle a complex professional task.

The idea is to evaluate models on tasks that reflect economically valuable work and have people with relevant expertise judge the results. That gives us a more practical signal of where models are capable and where they still need help. It’s not a complete measure of economic impact—doing a task isn’t the same as doing an entire job—but it helps narrow the gap between benchmark performance and usefulness in the real world.

r002.rationale: The response does not identify Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational task listings as a source for GDPval tasks.

r004.rationale: It says GDPval brings evaluation closer to useful work, but does not credit it with catalyzing greater organizational attention to that goal.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key question is: are models getting better at the kinds of work people actually need help with? A lot of benchmarks measure performance on questions with a clear right answer. That’s useful, but real work is often messier. You have to interpret a request, bring together information, and produce something that another person can actually use.

GDPval is an important step because it moves evaluation toward economically valuable tasks and the quality of the resulting work. That gives us a more practical way to understand both what models can do and where they still fall short.

It’s not a complete measure of economic impact. But it helps close the gap between a model getting a higher benchmark score and a model being more useful in someone’s day-to-day work.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention SWE-bench or say that it became saturated and obscured improvements between successive models.

r002.rationale: It refers broadly to economically valuable tasks but does not identify Bureau of Labor Statistics occupational task listings as the basis for selecting them.

r003.rationale: It describes real work in general terms but does not say models are evaluated on workplace tasks using the context available to a worker performing them.

r004.rationale: It says GDPval helps bridge benchmark scores and day-to-day usefulness, but does not credit it with catalyzing greater organizational attention to real-world usefulness.
